passage:
Sachin, can I tell you something weird? When I got into the design programme, I was sure they'd made a mistake. I'm Gurleen, the one whose portfolio got picked for the first-week display, and I still thought, any day now someone will notice I don't belong.
When Professor Nair praised my poster, I said, "Oh, I just got lucky with the colours." Then I stayed in the studio till two a.m. every night, redoing things nobody asked me to redo.
Last Friday, at the peer circle, I finally said it out loud: "I feel like a fraud here." I expected everyone to go quiet. Instead Meher said, "Same." Then Arvind said, "Me too, every single day."
Half the room had the same fear. It didn't disappear. But it got smaller, and I went home at eight that night.

qa.q: What did Gurleen say when Professor Nair praised the poster?
qa.a: "Oh, I just got lucky with the colours."

qa.q: What was Gurleen afraid of after getting into the programme?
qa.a: Gurleen feared being found out as not belonging, sure the programme had made a mistake.

qa.q: What helped Gurleen's fear get smaller?
qa.a: Naming the feeling aloud at the peer circle and hearing Meher and Arvind say they felt the same, which let Gurleen go home at eight.

qa.q: How might Meher and Arvind have felt when Gurleen spoke up?
qa.a: They were probably relieved to hear someone else say it, since they shared the same fear and had kept quiet about it too.

grounding: Shows a capable student who thinks success is luck, discounts praise and overworks, until naming the fear reveals peers feel the same.

passage:
Uday burst into the Kolkata flat waving a paper kite. "Maa! I made it myself! Look, the tail doesn't wobble anymore."
It had taken him four tries. The first three had torn or spun into the neighbour's balcony. This one had flown above the water tank for ten whole minutes.
He ran down to the rooftop again to show his friend Gurleen. She had brought her own kite, a shiny blue one, and hers flew even higher.
"Whoa, yours is so high!" Uday shouted, grinning. "How did you tie the string?"
Gurleen showed him the knot. Uday tried it on his kite, and it rose a little higher too.
That night he drew plans for a bigger kite, with a longer tail.

qa.q: How many tries did it take Uday to make the kite?
qa.a: Four tries.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when his kite finally flew?
qa.a: He felt proud and joyful; he burst into the flat waving it and wanted to show everyone.

qa.q: What does Uday's reaction to Gurleen's kite show about healthy pride?
qa.a: He was happy for her and asked how she tied the string, so his pride didn't need her to lose, and he learned something new.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when Uday cheers for her kite?
qa.a: Gurleen would likely feel glad and friendly, happy to share her knot with someone who is excited for her.

grounding: Shows a child glowing with pride in a kite he worked hard on, sharing it and celebrating a friend's success too.

passage:
When the arbiter announced the result in the Hyderabad community hall, Farhan closed his eyes and let out a breath. First place, city under-16 chess. He'd lost to the same opponent last year.
Ishita, the girl he'd beaten in the final, was packing her pieces slowly, jaw tight. Farhan walked over first. "Your knight sacrifice in round two, I didn't see it coming. You nearly had me."
She managed a small smile. "Next year."
"Next year," he agreed.
He found Coach Reddy by the door and touched his feet. "Thank you, sir. The endgame drills worked."
His friends wanted him to post the trophy photo everywhere. Farhan shrugged. "Maybe later." On the bus home, he held the trophy on his lap and grinned at nothing.

qa.q: Who did Farhan beat in the final?
qa.a: Ishita.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel on the bus home?
qa.a: He felt quietly proud and happy, holding the trophy on his lap and grinning to himself.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's actions showed pride without contempt?
qa.a: Going first to Ishita to praise her knight sacrifice and thanking Coach Reddy for the drills.

qa.q: What was it like for Ishita when Farhan came over?
qa.a: She was disappointed, packing slowly with a tight jaw, but his specific praise let her smile and look ahead to next year.

grounding: Shows a teen who wins a competition, enjoys it, thanks his coach and stays kind to the player he beat, without needing an audience.

passage:
Preeti, you know what I asked myself after the science fair? I'm Lalit, the one who came second, and I want to tell you honestly.
When they said my water filter was second and yours was first, part of me wanted to say yours was simple. I felt that ugly flash. So I asked myself: does my pride need you below me?
And the answer was, it shouldn't. My filter worked. I did well. And your solar dryer was genuinely clever. You did well too. Both things are true.
Then the judge said my data table had errors. Old me would have argued, or sulked for a week. I felt my face go hot, but I said, "Can you show me where?" She did. She was right.
So now I'm fixing the table. And I want to see how you built the dryer lid.

qa.q: What did Preeti build for the science fair?
qa.a: A solar dryer.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel when Preeti won first place?
qa.a: Lalit felt a flash of envy and wanted to call Preeti's project simple, but stopped to ask whether that pride needed Preeti below.

qa.q: How did Lalit handle the judge's correction wisely?
qa.a: Lalit felt embarrassed but asked, "Can you show me where?", listened, accepted the judge was right and started fixing the table.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel hearing Lalit say Preeti did well too?
qa.a: Preeti would probably feel respected and glad, especially when Lalit asks to see how the dryer lid was built.

grounding: Shows a teen checking whether their pride needs others below, crediting a rival's work and accepting correction without collapse.

passage:
Looking back at first year, I can see it now. Every story I told at the hostel table made me the hero. The time I "saved" the group project. The time I "basically taught" the coding club.
When Raghav got the internship I had applied for, I said, "That company's overrated anyway," and changed the subject to my own plans.
When our senior told me my presentation was disorganised, I went cold. I didn't speak to her for two weeks. Inside, though, I lay awake replaying it, feeling like a total failure.
That was the strange part. The louder I talked, the shakier I felt.
It was Raghav who said, gently, "Lalremsiami, you don't have to be the best in every story for us to like you." I was angry with him for a day. Then I wondered if he was right.

qa.q: What did the narrator say when Raghav got the internship?
qa.a: "That company's overrated anyway."

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after the senior's criticism?
qa.a: Lalremsiami acted cold on the outside but felt ashamed and insecure inside, lying awake replaying it like a total failure.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami try next, after Raghav's words?
qa.a: Lalremsiami could practise congratulating others sincerely and listening to criticism without going cold, perhaps talking the feelings through with Raghav.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when his internship was called overrated?
qa.a: Raghav may have felt dismissed and hurt, yet he still cared enough to say something gentle later.

grounding: Shows a young adult who casts themself as the hero, dismisses others' success and goes cold at criticism, while feeling shaky underneath.

subtype: Friend or partner on the receiving end [Receiver]
passage:
In the college counselling centre, Harish twisted his hands in his lap. "At first Rashmi said I was the smartest person she'd ever met. She'd tell everyone."
The counsellor nodded. "And now?"
"Now if I talk about my day, she changes the subject to hers. If she's late, it's my fault for 'rushing' her. Last week I got a good grade and she said, 'Must've been an easy test.'" He laughed, but it came out thin. "Maybe I'm too sensitive. Maybe I really am the problem."
"You've said 'maybe I'm the problem' three times today," the counsellor said gently. "What was it like before you met her?"
Harish was quiet. "I was sure of myself. I had friends I saw every week."
"Let's look at that together, over the next few sessions. And I'd like you to reconnect with one of those friends this week."
Harish nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did Rashmi say when Harish got a good grade?
qa.a: "Must've been an easy test."

qa.q: How does Harish feel about himself now?
qa.a: He feels small and full of self-doubt, wondering if he is too sensitive or really the problem.

qa.q: Why is talking with the counsellor an important step for Harish?
qa.a: A trusted outsider can help him see the pattern of being flattered, then blamed and unheard, before it wears down his confidence further.

qa.q: How does the counsellor see Harish's repeated "maybe I'm the problem"?
qa.a: The counsellor notices it as a sign of rising self-doubt and gently turns him toward how sure of himself he used to be.

grounding: Shows a young adult flattered early then made to feel small and blamed by a self-centred partner, recognising the pattern with a counsellor.

subtype: Setting boundaries with a self-focused person [Response]
passage:
For two years I kept trying to make Vikas see me. My cousin, same flat in Pune, same college. Every conversation became about him, and anything I shared turned into a joke at his next party.
I used to argue for hours: "That's not fair, you never listen." He'd just talk louder. I'd end up exhausted, still unheard.
This year I changed what I could. When he started mocking my exam stress, I said calmly, "I'm not discussing this with you," and went to my room. No debate. When he asked about my plans for the summer, I said, "Still deciding," and left it there.
He hasn't changed much. He still talks about himself nonstop. But I stopped expecting him to, and I stopped handing him things to use. I sleep better. Honestly, that was the part I could control.
Pradeep

qa.q: What happened to things Pradeep shared with Vikas?
qa.a: They turned into a joke at his next party.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel after arguing with Vikas for hours?
qa.a: Pradeep felt exhausted and still unheard.

qa.q: Which of Pradeep's new habits protected Pradeep's wellbeing?
qa.a: Staying calm, stating the limit "I'm not discussing this with you" without debate, and sharing less personal information, like saying "Still deciding."

qa.q: What would change if Pradeep kept expecting Vikas to change quickly?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely keep arguing for validation and end up drained, since Vikas hasn't changed much.

grounding: Shows a young adult setting calm limits with a self-focused cousin, sharing less and protecting their own wellbeing instead of expecting change.

Honestly? The first month at the agency was perfect. I'm Jyoti; everyone loved me. I brought samosas, remembered birthdays, made the boss laugh.
But after that, I figured I'd earned a bit of room. When Salma pitched the festival campaign idea in our small meeting, I polished it and presented it upstairs as mine. She'd never have sold it the way I did.
Now she's sulking. Last week she tried to tell me about her mother being in hospital, and I kept checking my phone. I mean, I asked the right questions when her brother turned out to know the client. That's just smart.

passage:
Okay, so you want to know how I handled Bidisha? I'm Leela, I work on the data team, and this went on for six months.
In meetings with the directors, Bidisha was warm and funny. Back at our desks, she'd say things like, "Leela's slides are cute, I'll fix them." Then she'd present my analysis as her own.
At first I was furious and wanted to outshine her in front of the bosses. That would have turned it into a contest.
Instead I started keeping records: dated emails, file histories, who did which chart. When she presented my forecast, I said calmly in the meeting, "Happy to walk through the method, since I built the model." I didn't insult her. Just the facts.
My manager checked the files. Credit got corrected. The rest of the team started doing the same, and the mood got better.

qa.q: What records did Leela start keeping?
qa.a: Dated emails, file histories, and who did which chart.

qa.q: How did Leela first feel about Bidisha taking credit?
qa.a: Leela was furious at first and wanted to outshine Bidisha in front of the bosses.

qa.q: Why was Leela's factual approach better than competing?
qa.a: It kept the focus on the work and the evidence rather than a popularity contest, so credit was corrected and team morale improved.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Leela offered to explain the method?
qa.a: Bidisha may have felt caught out and embarrassed in front of the directors, since the calm facts showed who built the model.

grounding: Shows a colleague observing a co-worker's credit-taking and responding with records and calm facts rather than competing for admiration.
